http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27926.text: Big News Network.com Ukrainian neo-Nazism is visible even to 'Russophobi' Poland - Putin The "foundations" of the current state have become a source of serious concern for Warsaw, the Russian president has said The neo-Nazi nature of the current Ukrainian regime has become so visible that even Polish authorities, who are gripped by Russophobia, cannot help but see it, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said. According to him, Poland simply cannot ignore the "obvious demand" of its own people to address the issue. Ukraine's open, state-sponsored glorification of World War II-era nationalists who collaborated with Nazis on multiple occasions and were responsible for the ethnic cleansing of Poles has driven a major wedge between Kiev and Warsaw. Earlier this month, Polish parliament speaker Wlodzimierz Czarzasty said that Ukrainians must "rethink all aspects of their history" and specifically recognize the massacre of Polish civilians at the hands of WWII-era nationalists as genocide before being greenlit to join EU. "Despite the well-known Russophobia in the politics of Poland, the Polish authorities today are nevertheless paying serious attention to the foundations of current Ukrainian statehood. I mean, first and foremost, the ideology of neo-Nazism," Putin told journalist Pavel Zarubin in an interview on Sunday, commenting on the situation. He added that the Polish leadership's "principled" position on the issue is a reflection of broad-based public demand. Earlier, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev also acknowledged what he called Warsaw's right attitude towards the rise of neo-Nazism in modern Ukraine. "However Russophobic the Polish elites may be, one cannot but admit that, on the issue of the repugnant Kyiv Bandera movement, they have taken the right and honest stance," Medvedev, who currently serves as deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, stated in a Telegram post in late June. He was referring to the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) - a WWII-era Ukrainian ultranationalist movement led by Stepan Bandera. The OUN collaborated with Nazi Germany during the early stages of its 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union. Its paramilitary wing - the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) - killed up to 100,000 ethnic Polish civilians in 1943-1944 in what is now western Ukraine, according to Warsaw's estimates. In accordance with laws passed following the 2014 Western-backed coup in Kiev, Ukraine officially banned both communism and Nazism and prohibited the public use of associated symbols, leading to the renaming of thousands of streets and cities. However, the same set of laws formally recognized the OUN and the UPA as independence fighters, despite their well-documented sponsorship by the Third Reich. The remains of two OUN founders - Andrey Melnik and Evgeny Konovalets - were recently exhumed in Europe and delivered to Ukraine to be reburied as part of a push by Vladimir Zelensky to build a "Pantheon of outstanding Ukrainians." Both men were known to have collaborated with Nazi Germany. In June, the Ukrainian leader also added the honorary title "Heroes of the UPA" to the name of an active commando unit, sparking outrage in Poland. Polish President Karol Nawrocki responded by stripping Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, his country's highest state honor, which had been awarded by his predecessor. Multiple Ukrainian officials, in turn, returned their Polish decorations in solidarity with Zelensky, while Polish officials returned Ukrainian awards. https://aa.com.tr/en/world/zelenskyy-say.text: RSS Diary Anadolu Ajansı © 2026 World Russia-Ukraine War Zelenskyy says US has given information to Ukraine about recent meetings in Moscow ‘We value alignment of steps and the fact that America is advancing a realistic vision of what needs to be done and what must be achieved,’ says Ukrainian president Burc Eruygur 29 August 2026 • Update : 29 August 2026 ISTANBUL Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the US had provided information to his country about recent meetings held in the Russian capital Moscow. During an evening video address late Friday, Zelenskyy said the information Kyiv received concerned meetings that took place in Moscow “the other day,” noting there was a “series” of them and that Ukraine spoke with the US before and after these meetings. “Thank you for the information – and for the necessary tone of the conversation with Russia. We value the alignment of steps and the fact that America is advancing a realistic vision of what needs to be done and what must be achieved,” Zelenskyy noted. “Russia must end its war, and all the necessary conditions must be created to make that happen,” he added, without specifying who took part in the meetings in the Russian capital. On Wednesday, the Kremlin confirmed reports that CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on Tuesday, the first visit by a CIA chief since 2021, saying it involved contacts between security services and describing such contacts as a "positive phenomenon, a positive process." The reports emerged after a US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III flew from the Latvian capital of Riga to Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport on Tuesday morning, according to Flightradar24. The aircraft had arrived two days earlier from Camp Springs in the US, near Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, where White House aircraft are often based. The aircraft departed Moscow and returned to Riga later the same evening, according to Flightradar24 data. Later on Wednesday, US President Donald Trump characterized Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow as "semi-routine." A day later, when asked in the Oval Office whether Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed or committed not to attack NATO territory, Trump replied: “I had good talks with him. He’s not going to be attacking a NATO territory.” Asked whether he wanted to deliver a warning to Russia not to attack NATO territory, Trump said: “I don’t want to comment on that, but they’re not going to attack.” news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All South Africa's president calls for new era in economic ties with India Russia says no mechanisms in place yet for economic cooperation with US Bahrain rejects participation in proposed Hormuz ministerial meeting with Iran China, India can achieve 'shared development,' Xi tells Modi in New Delhi talks Türkiye to host COP31 in Antalya in November 2026 Iranian president meets Abu Dhabi crown prince on sidelines of BRICS summit Egyptian president urges protection of international navigation amid regional tensions See All Ukraine says 37 killed in Russian drone strike on warehouse near Kyiv Venezuela’s ruling party backs oil deal with Washington, US Democrats skeptical

https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-p.text: WARSAW — European leaders are preparing to demand tougher sanctions on Russia at a summit on Thursday, putting them at odds with Donald Trump just days after the U.S. president struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports. The leaders plan to call for further sanctions and measures targeting Moscow's oil revenues at the European Council, according to a recent draft joint statement obtained by POLITICO, as EU governments reject Trump's claim to have secured an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. The disagreement exposes a widening divide over how to bring Moscow to the negotiating table. While Trump seeks to lower U.S. fuel prices by allowing more Russian diesel onto global markets, European leaders argue that restricting the Kremlin's energy revenues remains essential to forcing Putin to end the war. Advertisement Advertisement "Russia is not interested in deescalation, ceasing fire or peace," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a security conference in Warsaw on Monday. "That is why I will go to Brussels to ask my partners to consider seriously increasing sanctions against Russia." German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also called for further restrictions, pointing to Moscow's continued attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure despite Trump's announcement of a ceasefire. "Russia will only negotiate in good faith under pressure," Merz said Monday. "Following Moscow's reckless attacks on Ukraine's civilian energy supply, we must even tighten [sanctions] further." Friedrich Merz is pictured in Berlin on Oct. 12, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images The push follows EU foreign ministers' approval on Monday of the bloc's largest-ever addition to its Russia sanctions list, targeting almost 1,600 individuals and entities. The European Commission is also preparing a 23rd package of sectoral sanctions, which Kyiv expects to be circulated to EU governments by the end of the year, according to a senior Ukrainian official who was, like others in this article, granted anonymity to speak frankly on the sensitive negotiations. Other European countries are taking a similar position. Britain and Norway have also pledged to increase pressure on Moscow. "It's important to sanction Russia not to finance the war," Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO, calling for loopholes in existing restrictions to be closed. Advertisement Advertisement Trump's election calculation Behind closed doors, many European diplomats see Trump's abrupt shift toward easing restrictions on Russian energy as driven primarily by domestic political concerns ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections. That is the "broadly held view" among EU officials, according to one senior official. The president is under mounting pressure over fuel prices, which have surged since the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Having promised during his 2024 campaign to bring gasoline prices below $2 a gallon, Trump now faces an electorate paying more than twice that amount, with Republicans at risk of losing control of Congress. His agreement with Putin is intended to release an additional 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel onto global markets over the coming months, easing pressure on fuel supplies and prices. But European and Ukrainian officials question whether the additional supply will make a meaningful difference, saying that the total volume promised amounts to only around 10 days of U.S. demand. They feel the deal risks undermining efforts to deprive Moscow of the revenues funding its invasion. "The reality" is that the additional fuel will have a "minimal" impact on U.S. prices, the senior EU official said. Advertisement Advertisement "This is about the midterms," a second EU official said. "He said he would bring down prices, but then he decided to go to war with Iran." The officials also question whether Putin intends to honor Trump's purported energy ceasefire. Russia has continued striking Ukrainian energy infrastructure since the announcement, while Kyiv says it was not consulted on the arrangement. For now, most European officials are reluctant to criticize Trump publicly, despite any doubts about the agreement. The EU and Ukraine should maintain their position over the coming weeks, when the administration's longer-term intentions toward Kyiv may become clearer, one diplomat said, adding that Trump might even change course again if Putin fails to deliver the promised diesel. Pressure on Washington The dispute has also revived European calls for Washington to enforce its own sanctions against Moscow. Tusk urged Europe and the United States to act together to show Russia they were prepared to impose tougher measures, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called on Washington to align its approach with Brussels. Kallas pointed to sweeping Russia sanctions legislation championed by the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed into law last month but has yet to fully implement. Advertisement Advertisement The legislation gives Washington additional tools to target Russia's energy trade and those helping sustain its war effort. European officials want the administration to use them rather than loosen restrictions on Russian exports. Some Republicans are also calling for tougher action. "I think we need to be implementing the Russia sanctions bill," Republican Representative Dan Crenshaw told the Warsaw conference. The disagreement is raising wider questions in Europe about its dependence on Washington, particularly amid reports that U.S. officials have threatened to restrict Ukraine's access to American weapons unless Kyiv stops attacking Russian oil refineries. There is currently "no sign" Washington is following through on those threats, a NATO official told POLITICO, arguing that restricting sales would also hurt American weapons manufacturers. "PURL is a good deal for the Americans," the official said, referring to the NATO initiative under which European allies finance purchases of U.S. weapons for Ukraine. Advertisement Advertisement European Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius, without directly addressing the reports, said Europe needed to take "primary responsibility" for its own defense more urgently as Washington reduces its military presence on the Continent. The immediate test, however, comes on Thursday, when EU leaders will seek to maintain pressure on Moscow even as their most powerful ally moves in the opposite direction. Victor Jack and Sebastian Starcevic contributed reporting from Brussels, James Angelos contributed reporting from Berlin, Esther Webber contributed reporting from London.
